title: Mapping the World

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On 7 December 1972, one of the three astronauts on board the Apollo 17 spacecraft took a photograph. Released by NASA following the mission’s safe return from the moon, it showed, for the first time, the fully illuminated face of the Earth. Set against the cloud-streaked blue of the oceans, the outlines of Africa, Arabia and Antarctica were all clearly on display. Here, presented at last to the gaze of humanity, was a literally cosmic image of the geography of Earth.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Two and a half millennia earlier, an unknown clerk in what is now known as Iraq had sketched on clay the very earliest surviving attempt to represent the world. Iraq itself was placed at the centre of an encircling ring of oceans. Mountains, marshes and the river Euphrates: all were visible. Very clearly represented was the great city of Babylon. The concern of the clerk lay ultimately with what he would no doubt have seen as an altogether authentic dimension of reality. If the city of Babylon was placed at the centre of the map, then that was because the Babylonians took for granted that it was the central pivot of the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Then, in around 150 AD, an astronomer named Claudius Ptolemy wrote a book about how to make a proper map of the world. Penned in Greek on papyrus the work, known as the Geography, is one of the most famous ancient texts on the science of mapmaking. It placed the job firmly in the domain of the geographer, who could use astronomy and mathematics to calculate from the stars what the world looked like below. It recommended using geometric lines of latitude and longitude to convey a three-dimensional Earth on a two-dimensional surface, and it included the co-ordinates of over 8,000 locations in the ancient world. The Geography disappeared for a thousand years, only for a copy to appear in the 13th century, replete with maps drawn by Byzantine scribes. These geographic drawings, and all other maps based on scientific calculation, are Ptolemy’s legacy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Ptolemy’s scientific influence is explored in Jerry Brotton’s book A History of the World in Twelve Maps, which examines the complexity of mapmaking through the stories of 12 maps, which stretch across space and over time. In it he points out that Ptolemy’s scientific influence tells only part of the story. Mapmakers may be geographers, but they can also be artists and imperialists, storytellers and propagandists. All of which jostle with the science in determining what a map looks like and what it is used for. Brotton is a professor of Renaissance Studies at Queen Mary University of London, and the examples in the book are impressively varied, from Ptolemy’s toils to Google Earth, and include some Islamic and East Asian works that are less well-known to Western readers. However, bearing in mind that Brotton is a professor of Renaissance Studies, it is not surprising that the main part of his book should consist of a brilliant survey of mapmaking in the early modern period (the late 1500s to the mid-1700s). This is when Europeans began to explore entire continents unsuspected by Ptolemy. Despite their differences, the maps in this book enjoy some intriguing similarities, largely for the way they illustrate the priorities of their authors.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An example of such mapmaking priorities is that, even as recently as the 19th century, British mapmakers often placed the British Isles at the centre of maps. One such map in Brotton’s book features a view of the globe with Britain and the North Atlantic in the centre, to better portray the empire’s sea power, while Australia and half of South America are left off the map entirely. As Brotton notes, many of these maps, like those of the Spanish and Portuguese imperialists of the 16th century, did more to illustrate dominance and ambition than to improve mapmaking practice.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even now, when mapmakers have access to tools such as satellite images, there is still no objective and universally accepted map, argues Brotton. He goes on to say that Google Earth and other digital mapping applications are just as vulnerable as their predecessors to national priorities and cultural norms. As it is, those regions most exhaustively covered tend to be the ones with the highest concentration of computers and credit-cards.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is much to gain from this rich, if overly detailed book. However, Brotton’s survey of Ptolemy and the reaches of classical geography is only workmanlike and lacks the spark and the sense of the unexpected that elsewhere are features of the book. Considering that Ptolemy is the first of Brotton’s 12 mapmakers, this is unfortunate. Readers who find the first chapter dry are strongly urged not to cast the book aside, but to press on, because Brotton’s idea of tracing within maps the patterns of human thought and civilisation is a wonderful one.
